title: Optimizing benefit–cost ratios of hellbender reintroductions
content:
Given the possibility that Eastern Hellbenders will be federally protected throughout their entire range and the Missouri Distinct Population Segment has been protected since 2021, our work identifies a need to continue optimizing and validating reintroduction strategies that reduce economic costs while maximizing ecological efficacy. More broadly, our methodology represents a framework to aid decision-making in reintroduction science by integrating key demographic processes with economic considerations.


Abstract

Species reintroductions have emerged as a common conservation tool to combat global amphibian declines. However, given the mixed success of these efforts, it is important to weigh the potential benefits against the costs associated with different captive-rearing strategies. Here we perform a cost–benefit analysis of rearing and releasing different age classes of Eastern Hellbender (Cryptobranchus alleganiensis alleganiensis). Captive rearing has the potential to re-establish populations at historic sites and bolster populations in areas experiencing declines, but to date, there has been no critical evaluation of the optimal age and release numbers for achieving population establishment and their relative economic costs. Using demographic models and economic estimates from multiple captive-rearing facilities, we simulated releases into an unoccupied habitat and calculated the number of released individuals surviving to maturity and the associated cost of each reintroduction strategy. We show that the number of released individuals surviving to maturity increases with age of individuals being reintroduced, but rearing individuals for multiple years requires considerable economic investment. Despite the higher efficacy of releasing older individuals, releasing 3-month-old larvae was often more cost-effective (i.e. associated with the lowest per survivor cost) than releasing 3-year-olds and as cost-effective as releasing 1-year-olds, particularly when releases were spread across multiple sites to minimize mortality due to density dependence. Although we found evidence that larger facilities have cheaper per-individual rearing costs, thousands of animals must be reared to see appreciable economic benefits. Synthesis and applications. Given the possibility that Eastern Hellbenders will be federally protected throughout their entire range and the Missouri Distinct Population Segment has been protected since 2021, our work identifies a need to continue optimizing and validating reintroduction strategies that reduce economic costs while maximizing ecological efficacy. More broadly, our methodology represents a framework to aid decision-making in reintroduction science by integrating key demographic processes with economic considerations.
